Fig. 1: Motivating Examples. T2I editing methods like InstructPix2Pix [4] and FLUX.1 Kontext [33] can apply some semantics, but fail on others. This underscores the need for an automated approach to uncover the full range of editable semantics in generative models.

Fig. 7: Generalizability of Semantics. The top semantics discovered by RankT2I can be applied to edit different images (Base Model: FLUX.1 Kontext).

Fig. 3: Semantic Discovery for Real-Image Editing Using a Closed-Source Model. RankT2I finds both diverse and interpretable semantics in real images in many domains. GPT-Image-1.5 (see Footnote 1) was the base model that was used to generate these edits. The original images are from Unsplash (see Footnote 2).

Fig. 6: Comparisons with Other Attribute Retrieval Methods. RankT2I successfully identifies editable, diverse, and interpretable semantics compared to other attribute retrieval methods (e.g., first-K images, random selection, k-means, etc.).

Fig. 10: Generalizability of Woman Semantics. This image shows examples of the top 10 woman semantics discovered by our method using FLUX.1 Kontext and how they can be applied to edit different images.

Fig. 4: Top Discovered Semantics in FLUX-Based Models. RankT2I successfully identifies several semantics in FLUX-based T2I models compared to SliderSpace across various domains, including ancient ruins, planets, and cityscapes.

Fig. 2: An Overview of RankT2I. First, we prompt a multimodal vision-language model (MMVLM) [62] to obtain a list of potentially editable semantics for a domain. Then, we feed these semantics and a set of unedited images into a T2I model [3, 4, 33], to get a set of edited images. Lastly, we input the attributes list, unedited images, and edited images into our submodular framework, “RankT2I,” which suggests relevant, editable, and diverse semantics.
